sections.title: Level 2 Concept Overview
sections.content: At Level 2, simply memorizing the meaning of phrasal verbs is not enough. A single phrasal verb may have multiple meanings, and the correct meaning must be chosen according to the context. Additionally, some phrasal verbs look very similar to each other, so understanding the differences between them becomes important.

sections.title: Polysemy (Multiple Meanings)
sections.content: Step 1: Identify the phrasal verb. Step 2: Recall all its possible meanings. Step 3: Read the context of the sentence carefully and determine which meaning fits best. Step 4: Select the correct meaning accordingly. Example: 'make up' can mean invent (create a story), reconcile (end a quarrel), or constitute (form something). Sentence: 'He made up a story to avoid punishment.' Here the meaning is invent.

sections.title: Confusing Pairs of Phrasal Verbs
sections.content: Step 1: Identify both phrasal verbs. Step 2: Understand their separate meanings. Step 3: Analyze the sentence context. Step 4: Choose the one that logically fits the meaning. Example: break in = force entry or interrupt; break into = enter illegally. Sentence: 'Thieves broke into the house.'

sections.title: Separable vs Inseparable Phrasal Verbs
sections.content: Step 1: Identify whether the phrasal verb is separable or inseparable. Step 2: If the object is a pronoun (it, them, him), place it between the verb and the particle. Step 3: A noun object can sometimes appear either between the verb and particle or after the particle. Step 4: Avoid incorrect word order. Example: 'Turn off the light' or 'Turn the light off' are correct, but with pronouns 'Turn it off' is correct while 'Turn off it' is incorrect.

sections.title: Context-based Understanding
sections.content: Sometimes the meaning of a phrasal verb cannot be understood directly from the individual words. In such cases, reading the entire sentence carefully is necessary. The context of the sentence helps determine the correct meaning of the phrasal verb.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content: 1. Assuming that a phrasal verb has only one meaning. 2. Confusing phrasal verbs that look similar. 3. Using incorrect word order with pronouns.

sections.title: Quick Summary
sections.content: At Level 2, choosing the correct meaning of phrasal verbs depends on context. Similar-looking phrasal verbs can have different meanings, and the correct placement of objects is important in separable phrasal verbs.

tricks.title: Context Meaning Trick
tricks.explanation: A phrasal verb can have multiple meanings, so always read the entire sentence carefully.

tricks.title: Confusing Pair Comparison
tricks.explanation: Learn similar phrasal verbs together to clearly understand their differences.
tricks.example: Break in = enter by force, Break into = enter illegally.

tricks.title: Pronoun Position Rule
tricks.explanation: In separable phrasal verbs, the pronoun always comes between the verb and the particle.

tricks.title: Noun Object Flexibility
tricks.explanation: A noun object can sometimes appear either after the particle or between the verb and particle.
tricks.example: Turn off the fan / Turn the fan off.

tricks.title: Meaning Memory Groups
tricks.explanation: Memorize all common meanings of a phrasal verb together.

tricks.title: Similar Sound Alert
tricks.explanation: If two phrasal verbs look or sound similar, learn their meanings separately.
tricks.example: Pass out = faint, Pass away = die.

tricks.title: Sentence Logic Check
tricks.explanation: Choose the meaning that logically fits the sentence context.
tricks.example: He passed out due to heat. (fainted)

tricks.title: Particle Focus Trick
tricks.explanation: The particle (up, out, off, in) often changes the meaning significantly.
tricks.example: Take off = remove, Take up = start.
